title: Founded Pure Software to build debugging tools
statement: Hastings left Adaptive Technology in 1991 to found Pure Software, a company whose products troubleshot and debugged software, combining the debugging tool he had built at Adaptive with the focus lesson he credited to chief executive Audrey MacLean.
outcome: Rapid headcount growth outpaced his managerial experience and he asked his own board to replace him, saying he was losing confidence; the company nonetheless went public in 1995, merged with Atria Software in 1996, and the combined Pure Atria was acquired by Rational Software in 1997, after which Hastings left to start Netflix.

title: Co-founded Netflix as a flat-rate DVD-by-mail service
statement: Hastings and former Pure Software employee Marc Randolph co-founded Netflix on August 29, 1997, in Scotts Valley, California, combining DVDs, which were far easier to mail than VHS cassettes, with a website for ordering instead of a paper catalogue, and attaching the founding story of a forty-dollar Apollo 13 late fee and the gym-style subscription realization.
outcome: The service launched April 14, 1998 with a per-rental model, introduced a monthly subscription in September 1999, and dropped per-rental pricing by early 2000; by 2005 it offered thirty-five thousand films and shipped one million DVDs a day.

title: Pivoted Netflix to an all-you-can-rent subscription
statement: Fourteen months after launching with per-rental pricing, Netflix introduced a monthly subscription concept in September 1999 and dropped the per-rental model by early 2000, betting that a flat fee with no late fees would beat the store model whose economics rested on penalty revenue.
outcome: The subscription base scaled to a million DVDs shipped daily by 2005 on a thirty-five-thousand-title catalog, giving Netflix the predictable recurring revenue, customer data, and postal logistics that later funded the streaming transition.

title: Took Netflix public at fifteen dollars a share
statement: Netflix priced its initial public offering of 5.5 million shares at fifteen dollars, raising 82.5 million dollars, as an unprofitable online DVD-rental company in the wreckage of the dot-com bust, three months after dropping the dot-com suffix from its name.
outcome: Shares rose nearly twelve percent on the first day of trading to close at 16.75 dollars, which analysts called a good, successful offering in more sobering times; the company netted about seventy-five million dollars, paid off roughly fourteen million in debts, and kept expanding while Blockbuster test-marketed a rival subscription priced five dollars higher.

title: Launched the Watch Now streaming service
statement: Netflix launched streaming video on demand on January 16, 2007, with one thousand films available against seventy thousand on DVD, after scrapping a planned set-top box because YouTube's popularity convinced Hastings that the future was browser-based streaming on any screen.
outcome: Unlimited streaming was folded into disc subscriptions in January 2008, the abandoned player project became Roku, and by 2009 streams overtook DVD shipments, converting the free bonus feature into the core business that eventually attracted more than two hundred million subscribers.

title: Reversed the Qwikster split after an 800,000-subscriber loss
statement: Three weeks after announcing that the DVD business would be rebranded as a separate subsidiary called Qwikster, on top of a summer price increase that unbundled streaming and discs, Hastings cancelled the split and apologized, while keeping the higher prices.
outcome: Netflix ended the third quarter of 2011 with eight hundred thousand fewer United States subscribers, its first decline in years, and the stock plummeted more than twenty-five percent in after-hours trading; Hastings admitted overconfidence and moving too quickly, and the company slowed its decision-making to allow more internal debate.

title: Ordered House of Cards straight to series for two seasons
statement: Netflix outbid HBO, Showtime, and AMC for the Media Rights Capital political drama House of Cards, committing to twenty-six episodes across two seasons without a pilot, a decision driven by Ted Sarandos's reading of subscriber data showing an audience for Kevin Spacey films and David Fincher projects.
outcome: The first thirteen-episode season debuted February 1, 2013 as the first Netflix Original, released all at once in a binge format, and earned thirty-three Primetime Emmy nominations, making it the first original online-only streaming series to receive major Emmy nominations and establishing the originals strategy that grew into a seventeen-billion-dollar annual content budget.

title: Completed the succession to co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters
statement: Hastings announced that Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters would become co-chief executives of Netflix, with Peters promoted from chief operating officer and Hastings moving to executive chairman, after delegating management to the pair for two and a half years through what he called a baptism by fire of COVID and business challenges.
outcome: Netflix closed 2022 with 231 million paid memberships after adding 7.7 million customers in the fourth quarter, well above its 4.5 million forecast, and Hastings said he would spend more time on philanthropy while remaining executive chairman; in April 2026 the company announced he would step down from the board that June.
